item.title: Bomb fishing is wreaking havoc on Indonesia's coral reefs
item.description: 235 points, 128 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (e360.yale.edu)

→ HN comments  ·  235 points  ·  128 comments

Top #1 — wraptile:

I'm a scuba diver here in Thailand and you can still see blast fishing damage from decades ago that never fully recovered. It's truly as terrible as the article makes it out to be.

What is interesting is that both Indonesia and Thailand have strong and similar anti blast fishing laws since early 00s that charge 5+ years of prison time.

However, Thailand has been much more successful with taming blast fishing which is practically gone now and the story here is very insightful.

Some of it is due to Thailand's geography and high demand for marine tourism but the biggest push here was EU and US regulation that gave Thailand opportunity to shape up. In 2015 (same year when Thai anti blast laws were codified more strictly) US TIP (trafficking in persons) report down-graded Thailand to tier 3 mostly due to fishing slave workers while at the same time EU's IUU (illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing) issued a yellow card. All of which lead to the biggest fishery reform in Thai history which mostly eliminated blast fishing.

Since then Thailand is back to tier 2 of TIP and got lost the yellow card from EU's IUU. Indonesia never got tier 3 of TIP despite many arguing it should have and never got a card from IUU. Stories like this turn me into a globalization believer - I know it's not perfect but the system is kinda working?

↳ reply 1 — ghm2199:

Is it just a matter of incentives by the government in indonesia? Like is it that bomb fishing in indonesia is incentivized because of, for example, profit margins in fishing vs say tourism?

I know you mentioned Indonesia never got the yellow card it should have and that certainly creates less incentives for them to straighten their act. But I am trying to understand if the government is still largely to blame or not?

↳↳ reply — wraptile:

> But I am trying to understand if the government is still largely to blame or not?

all blast fishing is a failure of governance so I'd say yes but the fishing cultures here in SEA are so different from anywhere else in the world so it's very hard to govern without strong central body. Lots of cultural, religious, poverty and spiritual stuff mixed into all of that which really complicates things.

IMO Thailand has a much stronger centralized government and just better geography to make enforcement easier. It's mostly mainland with coastlines while Indonesia is mostly islands which are notoriously difficult to govern. So to answer your question, it's probably just that incentives in Thailand go much further due to all of these variables.

↳↳↳ reply — markdown:

While it's hard to regulate fishing when your country is made up of endless islands, it's quite easy to regulate dynamite. So no, I don't think the number of islands is an excuse.

In Fiji, for example, no fisherman could get dynamite if they wanted it. The only way to get that is if you run a (very heavily regulated) mine, or a quarry, and you'd have to account for every blast.

↳ reply 2 — throwaway2037:

Thanks for sharing your first-hand account of diving in Thailand. I think they should aggressively pursue coral planting. They are several projects in Indonesia that have demonstrated excellent results. I volunteered for a day doing coral planting in Bali, Indonesia. As part of the dive, they take you to different parts of the coral reef as it recovers, showing you how it changes year after year. You can see the change with your own eyes.

Top #2 — wlaw15:

Sometimes you learn of an unintended consequence of seemingly good idea wreaking havoc on an ecosystem. I would not put fishing with "plastic bottles filled with explosives" into that category.

Top #3 — willmeyers:

This is the repo if people are interesting in this work: https://github.com/ben-williams-ai/Bomb-Fishing

Author here. Thanks for the comments everyone!

There are many comments on the price point. I would like to comment on one thing.

"$20k is too much"

I agree $20k is an investment. Could I have done it for cheaper? Absolutely. Would a DIY shell been cheaper? Would doing more of the work myself have been cheaper? Could I have saved by putting in the smaller stock windows and not having a skylight? Of course!

But I am a dad with a young kid, he was 1 when I built the office. I didn't want to spend my limited free time on this project. There was a trade-off between paying for labor and the time it would take to do it myself. At this point in my life I always look at these decisions through a lens of: is the cost savings worth my time. In this case I valued my time more than the cost savings. I was lucky enough to be in a situation where I would rather spend money for someone else to build this then spending my nights and weekends on this project.

I am almost 4 years in I would have paid over $20k for a co-working space. We were able to stay in our smaller house with a ridiculously low mortgage rate. We made the right choice for us.

Cheap is relative. Sometimes your time is worth more. There are litteraly entire companies built on this premise, cough DoorDash

Even did off grid electric with solar to avoid needing contractors or permits. item.title: OpenAI Jalapeño: Better than Nvidia Blackwell
item.description: 246 points, 164 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (newsletter.semianalysis.com)

→ HN comments  ·  246 points  ·  164 comments

Top #1 — mchusma:

I think they talked about this being general purpose chip but I would think that Anthropic/OpenAI are at the scale now they could bake LLM weights into chips themselves.

For example, GPT Sol baked into a custom chip run for $100M that runs 10x as fast and 10x as cheap should pay for itself as long as the chip is useful for long enough.

While 2 years ago nothing was useful more than 1 year long, there are many older models in use now (e.g. Haiku 4.5, GPT-OSS 120b), and I expect this trend to continue.

I know this is what Taalas was doing (acquired by AMD), here was their demo, https://chatjimmy.ai/ which is based on Llama 3.1 8B. It feels like this should start to happen soon.

↳ reply 1 — bmulholland:

Probably! But not viable yet; the chips would be about a year behind SOTA. Note the ~16 months that the article quotes as being insanely fast to get this chip to tape-out (read: start producing). We'll have to bootstrap our way there: AI is actively being used to get us closer to viable lead times for this.

Unfortunately, there's some real physical constraints: IIRC, manufacturing a wafer takes on the order of a month, start to finish, for the physical processing.

Maybe once LLM improvements asymptote further?

↳↳ reply — kurthr:

The metal masked ROM is basically only 2 metal/contact layers. It's not a full new design and tapeout. You could roll a new set of parameters every ~2-3months. It's not an architectural change. See statements below.

https://www.eetimes.com/taalas-specializes-to-extremes-for-e...

https://www.turingpost.com/p/taalas

https://cambrian-ai.com/taalas-launches-hardcore-chip-with-i...

Part of the key is that by moving even from 6nm to 3-4nm one could embed a 20-30B model as part of a MoE (or only a subset of activated layers) on a single reticle die (note B300s are already multi-reticle), with a separate predictive/dispatch model controlling them each on a separate chip. This is without even stacking CiM ROM die. Moving the layer activations (and KV cache etc) between die requires relatively high speeds (and low latency), but distributed with multiple die in parallel might well be doable even with standard multilane PCIe. Of course KV cache prefill could also be handled by external GPUs. I'm sure AMD will make some reasonable choices.

↳ reply 2 — andy_ppp:

Yes, they could also sell me GPT Sol 5.6 or 5.7 on a chip and I’d probably buy it. It’s a really really useful model for me, I’m not sure how much better for coding I need it to be. For most things I find Sol good enough with a small amount of coaxing around my tastes.

↳ reply 3 — sebzim4500:

My guess is we only see this once they start saturating computer use benchmarks. That's a use case which would be extremely valuable at the right costs/speed, but the current models just aren't there yet.

Top #2 — jimmySixDOF:

↳ reply 1 — xyzsparetimexyz:

↳↳ reply — msh:

↳ reply 2 — Alifatisk:

Why censor yourself?

Top #3 — corford:

These nascent inference chip efforts are reminding me of the early 3dfx / riva / mach / powervr days. Will be interesting to see if inference chips are here to stay and, if so, who the eventual dominant player(s) will be

↳ reply 1 — ehnto:

Which in turn reminds me of Soundblaster audio cards! I suspect inference chips are closer to the GPU story than the Soundblaster story though.

I remember one soundblaster card I bought came with a Lara Croft demo, that exploited the incredible immersion of real time dynamic reverb.

Genuinely I think game audio took a few steps back from that heady era, the innovation in audio likely didn't sell as many cards as graphics innovations did.

↳↳ reply — bayindirh:

EAX was very powerful in its heyday, but it has died because of a thousand cuts.

First we had to have the audio processor. Good EAX was available on top of the line cards, and they were not always cheap. Lower end chips got less features.

Then we had to have the speaker setup to have the greatest sound, or needed to get a real 5.1 headphones, which were bulky and never provided the same fidelity.

Then Microsoft changed the Windows driver model, cutting the driver's direct access to the card. All of the timing sensitive effects were gone in an instant. I remember installing the new drivers and getting literally nothing. Sound Blaster was the only card with an hardware mixer, and Microsoft didn't feel like enabling them. Mixing at the DirectX layer killed the cards.

Soundblaster's very closed stance didn't help them either. None of the cards after Audigy2 worked with Linux when I had my desktop system.

After my Audigy2ZS, I moved to Asus Xonar D2X. Its positional audio capabilities were nice, but I mostly bought it for its Linux support and sound quality, and that was top notch in that regards.

Then sound cards became commodity. Everybody stopped making good cards. Musicians moved to audio interfaces, audiophiles moved to DACs.

Just looked to the SoundBlaster website. Internal cards are very limited. One DAC, one DTS enabled 7.1 sound card for PC cinema systems, three game oriented lower end cards, nothing else.

↳ reply 2 — wmf:

Every company is designing their own chips so the dominant players will be one level down: Broadcom, TSMC, Hynix/Samsung/Micron, etc.

item.title: Don't Wordle
item.description: 256 points, 109 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (dontwordle.com)

→ HN comments  ·  256 points  ·  109 comments

Top #1 — amiga386:

12935 -> TIZZY (5625) -> OXBOW (2674) -> GRUFF (858) -> MAMMA (195) and I'll let you guess the rest but my next choice left 43 words, and I survived with only 4 words possible.

The rules not letting use a letter you know isn't in the target word drastically cuts your choices, your best bet is to use as few unique letters per word as you can, and as uncommon letters as you can, but as all normal words need vowels you'll be forced into only picking a vowel from the target word soon enough. Try to find letters that are in the word as late as possible so you're not locked into having to use them.

Once you are forced to use letters from the target word, avoid placing them in the right place. Sadly there's a rule not letting you use a known letter more than once in a word (once A is known, you can't write ALPHA), and a rule for not letting you put a known letter in a place you know it doesn't go (so after MAMMA, you can't have HALVE because you know there's not an A in second place, nor ALPHA because you know there's not an A in fifth place).

↳ reply 1 — SkiFire13:

> Sadly there's a rule not letting you use a known letter more than once in a word (once A is known, you can't write ALPHA)

This is not entirely correct (or at least it's worded a bit weirdly).

If you know that A goes in a certain place you can still try a word using A more than once. It's only once you know that A does not appear twice (because you tried a word containing A twice, and the second A way gray!) then you can no longer use A twice.

In your case you tried MAMMA which contained 2 As and the second one gave you the information that there's no second A.

↳↳ reply — gpvos:

Are there no words with the same letter three or more times?

↳↳↳ reply — forbiddenvoid:

If there was a second of the same letter, but in the wrong place, it would be yellow. If it's gray, that means there is no repetition of that letter. So once you've seen that the second one is gray, you have the information you need to know that letter is not repeated.

↳ reply 2 — amiga386:

The best I could do with today's word, and the wordlist, but no scoring function to minmax the rules:

- FUFFY (8159) (shipping of Faith and Buffy from Buffy the Vampire Slayer)

- IMMIX (4544) (to mix or blend)

- QAJAQ (530) (alternative form of kayak)

- TRATT (155) (clipping of trattoria)

- KHAPH (7) (alternative form of khaf, the 11th letter of the Hebrew alphabet)

I get the feeling that if this game had 7 steps instead of 6, it would almost always be impossible.

↳ reply 3 — gowld:

> Sadly there's a rule not letting you use a known letter more than once in a word (once A is known, you can't write ALPHA),

That rule doesn't make sense.

What if the answer is AORTA, and you want to guess ALBUM and then ALPHA?

If you enjoy clicking things you can spend hours in their cookie consent boxes untickinv the several hundred individual ‘legitimate interest’ tick boxes for individual vendors

↳ reply 1 — wlesieutre:

  We and our 1022 partners…

Instead, just dismiss the banner however and clear the site's cookies in the browser when you're done. On Firefox, you can clear your cookies in 3 clicks, use the little button on the left side of the URL bar and hit "Clear cookies and site data" and then Confirm.

item.title: Credit Card Rewards Became a $9.2B Wealth Transfer
item.description: 141 points, 273 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (library.hbs.edu)

→ HN comments  ·  141 points  ·  273 comments

Top #1 — nsedlet:

Credit cards also transfer wealth from people who pay interest to people who don’t.

It’s a silly system, where everyone has to invest their time (optimizing for rewards, avoiding interest) in an ultimately negative sum game. I hate it so much.

↳ reply 1 — delish:

Patrick McKenzie rebuts this here: (podcast) https://open.spotify.com/episode/2E2KRPcDvh1LcRw5bIsBms or here (article): https://www.bitsaboutmoney.com/archive/anatomy-of-credit-car...

The intuition being: people who carry balances and pay interest don't actually spend very much; they are not wealthy.

↳↳ reply — buran77:

What does that graph tell you? Because I think patio11 wanted to send one message and people accidentally misunderstand the graph.

That's the interchange income corresponding to wealthy people. Interchange is paid by the card-accepting business, not by the buyer. The buyer pays interest and other fees and that graph looks very different.

From that original study the full picture table says in % of ADB that the "poorest" (below 620 FICO) pay ~45% interest and fees but bring only 2% additionally in interchange income. The wealthy (at 800+) pay ~10% interest and fees but bring another almost 10% interchange income, on 4 times higher spending, and 3 times higher rewards (so the wealthy get ~12 times higher rewards in $ value than the "poor").

Just the percentages paid by each group more than offset the difference in spending. There are also way more "poor" accounts than wealthy accounts. Intuitively you can tell that the banks are effectively subsidizing the fees and interest for the wealthy with the income from the poor, for the sake of the interchange income which is mostly generated by the wealthy but doesn't come from their pocket.

Those poorest of people (<620 FICO) pay more interest and fees (percentage and absolute terms) than any other group. There's a range in the middle on the wealth scale where the customers are actually a net loss for the banks (the 660-760 FICO range).

↳↳↳ reply — tylerhou:

Businesses raise prices to account for interchange fees. So they are essentially is paid by the consumer. If we outlawed rewards credit cards (by capping interchange fees), everything would likely be slightly cheaper.

↳ reply 2 — nerdjon:

I gave up long ago trying to optimize any rewards, it just ended up being stressful and not really worth it ultimately.

Now I just use my apple card everywhere, pay it off every month and get whatever rewards I get.

It feels like a weird situation, those that stand to gain the most from credit cards are also the ones that should feel a difference of under $100 in rewards the least.

The one exception I see is bonus sign up rewards since those can be fairly significant, or making sure you use an airline card at the airline since those bonuses can be fairly significant (with sometimes other benefits). But outside of those exceptions, just choose a card with good rewards and stick with that and pay it off every month.

↳ reply 3 — ramijames:

I'm 46. I've never had a credit card. I have a bank account and a debit card. If I can't afford something, I don't buy it.

You can just opt out of using credit cards.

Top #2 — SXX:

Important context: this is US thing. EU capped interchange fees at 0.2% for debit and 0.3% for credit cards.

So in US card processing is x5-x10 more expensive.

↳ reply 1 — tiffanyh:

To be more specific, this is a US credit card topic.

Debit card fees are capped in the US, yet I’ve never received a discount from a merchant for paying with debit instead of credit.

As such, I just pay with credit and have never understood this argument.

↳↳ reply — post-it:

That's what makes it a wealth transfer, from debit card users to you.

↳↳↳ reply — iso1631:

In my country card fees are less than cash fees, so I guess that's a wealth transfer from card payers to cash payers?

↳ reply 2 — gorgmah:

It's partly true: this only applies to consumer cards. That's why many EU banks still offer corporate credit cards with huge cashback etc. For example, revolut offers no cashback in France on their metal cards if you have a consumer account, but up to 1% cashback on the same card if you have a "freelance" account. https://www.revolut.com/fr-FR/metal/

Second thing: interchange fees are not the only fees that your typical store has to pay, the total fees are much higher. I think the EU essentially capped Visa/Mastercard profit in the EU, more than they capped small business fees for card payment.

Top #3 — roland35:

Patrick McKenzie (patio11 fame) had a great blog post in credit card rewards

There is a lot that goes into it, and it is interesting how customers like me who literally never have carried interest and have to made thousands of $ in rewards over the years still make the banks money....

https://www.bitsaboutmoney.com/archive/anatomy-of-credit-car...

↳ reply 1 — steveBK123:

Credit card points/miles are an interesting topic, and I have found them to be kind of useful cyclically myself over last 20 years.

They are a way for airlines to create value out of thin air with their own fiat currency. For the average consumer the miles create less of a pure economic efficient benefit and more of a psychic benefit - funny money bucket that accumulates to defray some trip expenses. Economically they'd be best off with an outright 2% back card.

For the minority of customers who are flexible on dates/locations and willing to plan in advance - most airline/hotel programs have sweet spots at the more premium level.

I use them to fly overseas business class refundable fares at discount. It's not free, but the taxes paid + foregone $ I could have gotten with a cash-back card ends up being 2-3x economy non-refundable fare instead of the 5-7x listed cash price if I bought the business class ticket outright.

It's generally a time-vs-money thing though in that to maximize airline/hotel programs you need to pay attention to various limited time offers for signup bonuses, spending bonuses, conversion bonuses, redemption bonuses, etc. Without those it's a very uphill battle.

↳↳ reply — nickjj:

> It's generally a time-vs-money thing though in that to maximize airline/hotel programs

Credit card hotel booking portals are often much worse than what's available too.

For example, you might end up paying 30-100% more for a hotel booked through Chase Travel. At the very least you'll have way less selection. Even if price matching exists, you could still end up paying more.

I am traveling to Mexico next month and I do have a Chase Sapphire Preferred card (the one with the $95 annual fee). You get $100 in hotel credits per year if you book through Chase Travel.

In one of the spots I'll be at, there was (1) selection. It was $92 for 2 nights in a pretty low populated town that I'll be passing through. That hotel was rated 3.2 stars on Google.

If I use Google search or any hotel aggregator site, there were over 10 hotels available for half the price with much better ratings.

In this case it cost me about $50 extra to use the card's benefits.

Many people don't understand how rewards work when it's marketed towards your annual fee. The $100 credit doesn't offset the $95 annual fee. You pay $95 out of pocket for the fee. As soon as you book that hotel for $100 you've now paid $195 total out of pocket of which $100 gets credited back, so you're still out $95. If you instead didn't have the card and got the hotel at the cheaper rate, you'd only be out $45 or whatever you paid.

I mainly got the card because it had a really good sign up bonus, 0% international exchange fees and reasonable rental car coverage. Other cards can cover these benefits without an annual fee.

↳ reply 2 — swed420:

Discussion of patio11's article:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39928604

item.title: Why some US restaurants are banning tips
item.description: 178 points, 370 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (bbc.com)

→ HN comments  ·  178 points  ·  370 comments

Top #1 — palata:

> the problem of going tip-free is that customers struggle to get their heads around the maths.

Maybe they should show the price "without tip" next to the full price, so people can compare.

Paying employees with tips is an insane concept, fundamentally abusive. If it wasn't, then the owner would also get paid from tips. "The meals are all free, and we count on you to pay them through tips". Obviously no owner would take that risk, because it is insane. They make their employees take that risk because they can abuse them, that's all.

↳ reply 1 — OkayPhysicist:

The entire point of tips is that they are the workers', 100%. It's also a variable cost based on the willingness to pay, so it creates a form of price discrimination, where those willing to spend more, spend more, those wanting to spend less, spend less.

Those two factors lead to the inescapable conclusion that tipped staff make more money. Price discrimination captures surplus value that simply is not available to schemes that don't use price discrimination, and any new price discrimination scheme would almost certainly benefit the employer at least in addition to the employees, if not be entirely captured by the owners.

Combined with the, let's say "extra judicial tax incentives", non-tipping restaurants simply cannot compete with tipping-norm restaurants for service staff. In an environment where tipping exists everywhere else, you then get an adverse selection pressure for shitty waitstaff, because if they were competent they would be working somewhere that competency would earn them tips. Which piles on top of the dealignment of incentives to create substantially lower quality service.

↳ reply 2 — tdeck:

> If it wasn't, then the owner would also get paid from tips.

Actually it's quite common for owners to take some of the tips, even though that's not legal.

Top #2 — walrus01:

We need to at least normalize not tipping for counter service. Given the current wage structures and labor laws in the US and Canada, if I sit down at a table and I receive table service, I'm going to tip 15% unless the service was abhorrent.

I am not going to tip if I order and take my food from a counter and serve myself (and then almost certainly clear my own table as well), or I buy any other form of product standing up. Basically, if I'm standing for the entire customer service transaction, it's not tippable.

↳ reply 1 — Tyr42:

And you are tipping before you even see the service in that case, as you pay before the food.

Of course, the staff also see how you tio before they prep your food...

↳↳ reply — walrus01:

↳↳↳ reply — account42:

Is that really typical though? IME there are more places where you order and pay and then wait for your food to be made than there are places where your food gets put together while you are ordering and you pay afterwards.

↳ reply 2 — joenot443:

What are the Canadian labor laws you're referencing?

To my knowledge, the only province which still has the "liquor server" minimum wage is Quebec - everywhere else gets the same minimum wage as other workers.

To be clear, a server in Ontario is not legally allowed to be paid any less than $17.60/h _plus_ their tips.

Top #3 — Rygian:

As a foreigner in the US, I've made the faux-pas of assuming waiters and waitresses were being paid a full salary by their employer.

I even suspect that I received sub-par service from some of them, who may have identified me as a "no-tip risk" from the first moment.

↳ reply 1 — raegis:

> As a foreigner in the US, I've made the faux-pas of assuming waiters and waitresses were being paid a full salary by their employer.

This depends on the state. For example, in California, servers get state minimum wage, at least ($16.90/hour). On the other hand, most "red" states use the federal minimums: $2.13/hour for servers (!) and $7.25/hour for non-tipped employees.

↳ reply 2 — snayan:

I'm not saying they're right to do so, but it sounds like their intuition was honed well if they pegged you correctly during your faux-pas era? Fascinating, wonder what the tell was.

item.title: Windows 95 released August 24, 1995
item.description: 125 points, 90 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (dfarq.homeip.net)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  90 comments

Top #1 — 1970-01-01:

>It wasn’t truly a full 32-bit operating system, because there was still MS-DOS at the core if you dug deep enough.

Yes it wasn't truly 32-bit but the core was not MS-DOS. It was a hybrid. The Win95 kernel was 32-bit and drove almost all of the system, including memory. 16-bit DOS was used as a launching pad and then it's job shifted to handle 16-bit graphics and other hardware that was unable to work with the new 32-bit kernel. So you booted 16-bit DOS, and as WIN.EXE executed, the system transmorphed from 16-bit into a 32-bit (kernel) OS but some of that core 16-bit driver code was designed to remain welded onto it. Even more impressive is how you could dissolve this 32-bit level and return the system to 16-bit DOS. That remains a very impressive achievement 30 years later. Happy anniversary Windows 95!

↳ reply 1 — TazeTSchnitzel:

The way Windows 95 could use DOS device drivers despite being 32-bit was fairly incredible. I think that fooled a lot of people into thinking it really was running on top of DOS, when in reality, once it has booted, the reverse is the case. https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20071224-00/?p=24...

↳ reply 2 — mananaysiempre:

It’s not correct to say it was “really 16-bit”, no, but as Unauthorized Windows 95[1] eloquently demonstrates, neither was Windows 3.1 or 3.11, especially with Win32s, and Windows 95 was much more of a direct descendant of that environment that the marketing implied.

And on a more personal note, reading the descriptions of the mixed 16/32-bit architecture always makes me feel conflicted.

On one hand, the technical achievement is somewhere between genius and madness and I’m not sure on which side—not only did they ship a hypervisor in a consumer OS in 1987 (as “Windows/386”), they also flipped a live MS-DOS with an unknown complement of drivers and binary patches from running on live hardware to running inside a(n admittedly unsafe) VM, then proceeded to use those drivers and respect the patches including in applications written for Windows and not MS-DOS. I don’t think I have the sort of arrogance it takes to even think of attempting such acrobatics.

On the other hand, I was there, I grew up on computers that ran Windows 95 and 98, and I remember just how much better Windows 2000 was, how much more comfortable it was to not worry about the system crashing on you every half an hour. Perhaps 95 was a magnificent technical achievement, but it certainly didn’t feel like one to the user. And thus I continue to feel conflicted.

There’s also the question of why, exactly, was NT too heavy to run on contemporary consumer machines. You could say it was bloated, but so was Windows 95: the multiple 16/32-bit mode transitions it took to write to a file certainly weren’t free; and don’t get me started[2] about shipping a COM-based shell, realizing it was too heavy for the minimum RAM requirement, and solving that by shipping a second, stripped-down copy of COM then live-swapping the real one in its place as soon as the fake one became insufficient.

[1] https://www.os2museum.com/wp/book-review-unauthorized-window...

[2] https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20040705-00/?p=38...

↳ reply 3 — luckystarr:

I noticed back in the days that my FidoNet point client software ran a lot faster (actually processing a lot of messages, so IO and CPU heavy) in Windows than in DOS, which was unintuitive to me back then.

Top #2 — ramijames:

I remember being 15, that August. We were excited for this release. My dorky friends and I went to a local computer store and tried to get the clerk to show us what Windows 95 was like. He had a pre-release version installed on one of their computers. I don't even remember how we knew.

The clerk refused to show us. I'm still irritated about it.

↳ reply — TZubiri:

Funny to think of W95 like some kind of luxury that a shopkeeper has to keep teenagers out, as if you were trying to test drive a Mercedes, or trying out guitars like that scene from Wayne's World (1992)

↳↳ reply — ssl-3:

Or maybe the PC was in the back of the shop, in some non-public area that a bunch of random, inquisitive people (regardless of age) weren't welcome to visit.

Maybe the area was just trashed or otherwise unseemly, and would leave a bad impression. Maybe the shopkeeper smoked weed back there and didn't want to expose kids to Bertha, his prized six-foot bong. Who knows.

When I've worked in shops that sold electronics with a retail storefront, we tried to keep the showroom looking very nice and uncluttered. The back rooms where we repaired stuff and tinkered around with gear were very different: These were utilitarian spaces that regular customers weren't often invited to see.

Nothing particularly untoward ever went on back there, but still: There's reasons why shops (of all sizes) have interior walls. :)

↳↳↳ reply — ramijames:

Ya, I'm sure the guy had his reasons. We were just kids. It's not like we were going to be buying a $4k computer. We were just a nuisance.

Top #3 — p0w3n3d:

My memories of windows 95 are very fond. I used to install it on Pentium 133 and boy it flew.

However the most wonderful thing about software written at that time was it was written with care and skill.

item.title: SiFive's First Server Platform
item.description: 127 points, 40 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (chipsandcheese.com)

→ HN comments  ·  127 points  ·  40 comments

Top #1 — yjftsjthsd-h:

> Support for double-wide GPUs (Up to 450W)

I wonder how the driver situation is. From Jeff Geerling's work on running "big" GPUs on Raspberry Pis, my impression is that often less-common platforms should work but are littered with papercuts in practice.

↳ reply 1 — jogu:

AMD GPUs have worked on RISC-V for a couple years at this point. I have a Milk-V Titan that's paired with an AMD GPU running well: https://milkv.io/titan

↳↳ reply — sylware:

Maybe a Zen microarchitecture with a RISC-V/RVA front-end?

While thinking about it, if NVIDIA or SAMSUNG go performant RISC-V CPU micro-architecture, will "probably" change the world.

↳ reply 2 — geerlingguy:

Somehow the RISC-V designs mostly seem to have more coherent PCIe implementations, meaning some devices are easier to get running without the arm64 quirks drivers have to work around.

Drivers still need tweaking, most of the time, since most are still built assuming an amd64 world.

↳ reply 3 — cultofmetatron:

> Support for double-wide GPUs (Up to 450W)

oh a double wide surprise for the AI industry? just what we needed.

Top #2 — camel-cdr:

https://camel-cdr.github.io/rvv-bench-results/sifive_p870/in...

Top #3 — ComputerGuru:

Not to knock on RISC-V, which I’ve been following from the embedded side of things for many years now, but I feel I must question the value of a license-free ISA in this specific market segment at this time.

Surely between the squeeze on RAM and storage pricing and the exorbitant costs of training or mass-inference scale GPUs (if you’re going into AI), the nominal cost of the CPU licensing is really not going to make or brake anything or unlock some new business viability?

Even RISC-V aside, we are essentially in a position that would have been impossible to even dream of ten or twenty years ago when Intel was the only player in the game.

Wouldn’t buying off-lease hardware (not even in bulk) give you better performance per dollar, better compatibility, and more options?

Not to say any of this will always be the case; even if RAM pricing doesn’t come down, storage will, and RISC-V processors will (maybe) eventually actually be competitive when it comes to SOTA performance, but today in 2026?

↳ reply 1 — hedora:

The promise of RISC-V is probably not that it cuts pennies of a $1 embedded ARM core (or dollars off a $100 core).

Instead, it’s that Moore’s law keeps on trucking along, so now we have lots of dark silicon (you cannot turn the whole core on at once, or it will turn into a puddle of glass) and specialized silicon.

RISC-V removes all the gatekeepers (except TSMC and the other fabs) that historically blocked new specialized silicon.

I could get an ARM license, but suspect that, at best, that means dealing with sales folks and also building out a legal division just to manage the license.

I could be wrong, but it’s easier to go with the open core, in the same way that I suspect I cannot afford to figure out how much I would have to pay in order to license windows for my servers.

↳ reply 2 — zamadatix:

The article doesn't put much emphasis on it, but like it says this is still a development system. It's not intending itself to be competitive with ARM and x86 servers for the typical server buyer in 2026.

item.title: Thomson Reuters Launches Its Own Frontier Model
item.description: 125 points, 52 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (thomsonreuters.com)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  52 comments

Top #1 — underlines:

Please challenge me and explain why this is a break through worth the headline they use for their own work.

How I understand it, without really reading into it:

- Thomson Reuters did not "create" a frontier model, they gave some money, maybe a bit of their data to Imperial College London, and took Alibaba's Qwen 3.6 35B A3B Model for a basic fine tune.

- "They" (some undergrads at Imperial College London) used an existing ablation framework to undo some of the topic alignment of the original model.

- "They" fine tuned on some domain knowledge trying to preserve general knowledge - here maybe, just maybe some data came from Thomson Reuters.

As a result: one of 100's of Qwen 3.6 35B A3B sparse model fine tunes, just for publicity, to write overstating headlines like "X created their own frontier model"

item.description: 126 points, 214 comments. See description for top comments.

Top #1 — tpurves:

Literally the best possible kind of psy-op. Same with translating Sesame Street and distributing it to 100s of countries. Same with countries like Thailand exporting Thai food. It's a psy op based on what if we took nice things from our country and subsidized distributing them to the rest of the world, our country would grow in prestige and soft power. And these strategies are usually pretty effective, not to mention usually net-positive for all sides ... compared with so many other horibble harms US and other countries foreign offices have done around the world out of self interest.

↳ reply 1 — scarecrowbob:

↳ reply 2 — foolinaround:

↳ reply 3 — lo_zamoyski:

Or the appearance of nice things. Consider the suburb as promoted by American film which has left a very deep mark on the global imagination and that, regrettably, maintains a strong influence over housing markets and urban planning to this day.

Top #2 — ivan_gammel:

Not the first time when the Default Country thinks they invented everything. The title is almost comical.

Modern art, as everyone should know, started in 1860s in Europe inspired by technological advances, globalization of trade and cultural exchange. Japanese art made huge blast, photography pushed to seek new forms of expression, social progress demanded new messages and new images. We had impressionism, post-impressionism, then the whole explosion of artistic forms and ideas in 1910s-1930s. All of that was Modern Art.

CIA was founded in 1947 and CIA-sponsored soft power projection was a relatively short period in the world history lasting just a few decades, a part of the bigger game played between the USA and the Soviets, which did exactly the same (and thanks to whom we have now e.g. Studio Ghibli).

↳ reply 1 — coldtea:

Sure. But those making the claim are not talking about that.

They're talking about the post 50s abstract expressionism and pop art movements.

Just because it says "modern art" doesn't mean it refers to any and all modern art, much less 19th century art or say cubism or dada.

↳ reply 2 — rdtsc:

I think you might be reacting to the title only. The claim in the article is better phrased as “the Modern art was psy-op-ed by the US govt, especially through CIA”. They didn’t invent it, they may not even liked it personally. The very same artists making these paintings were not too far from being left leaning and sympathizing with regimes and ideas US government fought against. Nevertheless, it was still worth it, the sponsorship was seen as a counter to the Soviet art and culture. If anything a least as a “look you can even create these crazy paint splatters in a free society and nobody sends you to gulag” kind of angle.

Top #3 — coldtea:

A lot of people are confused by the term "modern art" in this.

This isn't meant to be about the idea of modern art in general, not about modernist art, or a "history of art" compatible conception of the term.

So whether "modern art started with the invention of the film camera" and other such claims about the late 19th here is irrelevant.

In the context of TFA and the CIA-related discussion, "modern art" refers mainly to abstract expressionism and to a lesser degree pop art and conceptual art, in US and Western Europe.

That was the scene and its sub-scenes which dominated the Western galleries and art world in the post "cold" war period, and for layman uses (and even for several critical treatments), it was synonymous with modern art, in the sense of the fine arts, in general. Hence the use of the term.

That's the way the term "modern art" is used in this.

item.description: 133 points, 50 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  133 points  ·  50 comments

Top #1 — philips:

If it is helpful to other people here is how I manage my ebook library with flatfiles and heterogeneous devices (Android, macOS, iOS, Kindle, etc)

I have my own eBook library hosted with copyparty. It is a single binary. Runs on plain files. And speaks OPDS for integration with KOreader (Kindle) or Readest (iOS/macOS). https://github.com/9001/copyparty#opds-feeds

It also speaks webdav so I can quickly sync everything via rclone to an SD card on devices like an Android tablet.

I really like the convenience of flat files and multiple protocols.

↳ reply — ukz:

Copyparty is super cool, it can also be configured to use S3 backend.

How do you manage your reading progress?

Top #2 — phildenhoff:

Having built a tool in this space, I enjoy seeing all the Calibre alternatives that have been coming out in the last few years! It's fascinating to see the specific wants that people have.

Bookshelf, for example -- what possesses someone to make an ebook library that _only works on object storage_? Is this a weekend project, answering the question of "what would this look like"? Or was it something the author wanted for a long time?

↳ reply — PurpleRamen:

> Having built a tool in this space, I enjoy seeing all the Calibre alternatives that have been coming out in the last few years!

If there would be just anything actually good. But for some reason they all have just very basic organisation-levels, and barely any support for handling custom data from calibre.

For some reason, streaming ebooks seems to be also not existing. One can either download the whole book, or use some lousy in-browser-reader. So strange how the ebook-world has no decent software for selfhosting.

Top #3 — bordercontrol:

Client side end to end encryption is a must have for me when hosting anything nowadays. I am using Cryptomator for this specific reason. It takes away a lot of legal questions because I only need to curate the data to serve my own needs and do not have to curate it for state actors too.

I really wish client side end to end encryption would become more widespread in the developer community. It is not hard to implement anymore and takes away all the headaches of having to comply with certain regulations.

There are so many laws now that regulate copyright and hosting. An accidentally public S3 bucket full of ebooks could technically land you in jail in certain jurisdictions. Automatic shutdown notices. Providers themselves may also automatically scan stored material, and so on. There are so many reasons not to host your media library unencrypted on a third party server.

I recommend using this kind of tool only if you can prove that you are legally allowed to possess every ebook you upload in every jurisdiction you travel to or live in, as well as in the jurisdiction where the server is located.

RIP Aaron Swartz.

↳ reply — phrotoma:

Appreciate this suggestion, cryptomator seems super cool and I had not heard of it until reading your comment.

item.title: One corner of China’s internet is insisting that the Tang Dynasty never existed
item.description: 154 points, 132 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cnn.com)

→ HN comments  ·  154 points  ·  132 comments

Top #1 — A_D_E_P_T:

There are primary sources. There are archeological sites: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qianling_Mausoleum

There are also histories written just after the Tang Dynasty had fallen. It was considered good form for a new dynasty to write a historical review of the previous one, and there are two retrospectives on Tang, e.g.: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Book_of_Tang

And there is ironclad evidence from foreign sources. Among others, Japanese histories detail the journeys of emissaries to the Tang Court: https://web.archive.org/web/20260315181529/https://japansoci...

So the theory is bait, and hard to take seriously.

But I'll give it credit for hijacking a genuinely interesting scholarly premise: What is taken quite seriously is the notion that China's first dynasty -- the Xia Dynasty -- never existed. It is of rather mythic proportions; later Chinese would speak of Xia the way Romans would speak of Troy. And there is very little evidence to support its existence. The Shang Dynasty is also supported by rather scant evidence -- and is also mythic, though obviously less so than the Xia.

Worth noting that both the Xia and Shang are exceedingly ancient -- roughly 2000 BC to 1000 BC between them -- unlike the Tang, which fell around 900 AD and is thus middle-of-the-pack by Chinese dynastic standards.

↳ reply 1 — senderista:

The Shang dynasty is also kind of a propaganda nightmare, with all the archeological evidence for mass human sacrifice.

↳↳ reply — A_D_E_P_T:

Yeah. You're probably familiar with the "Hanfu" revival -- a sort of resurgence in people adopting traditional clothing and makeup styles from the Han and Tang dynasties. It's entirely on account of the fact that those two dynasties were remarkably stable, prosperous, and peaceful, so they lend themselves to historical romanticism -- like the Chinese equivalent of the Renaissance Faire. Good vibes. Even popular in Japan, with e.g. The Apothecary Diaries and similar fare.

Shang, and all of the post-dynasty collapse centuries like The Spring and Autumn Period, were not great times to live in. Dismal and evil vibes, for the most part, unless you happen to be a mighty hero or bandit-lord who believes that he can conquer the age. Even so, most of them ended up in soup pots.

> Even popular in Japan, with e.g. The Apothecary Diaries and similar fare.

But we build resources like Wikipedia and science journals, which also use disagreement as an engine for generating a more correct understanding. Its a strange and hopeful aspect of human societies.

They claim the panama canal is continuously fed by freshwater for the canal locks (which segment the canal into sections with different water levels, and which enable ships to be raised or lowered to the next water level during travel along the canal).

It's 2026, why are humans dumping freshwater into the oceans? This can perfectly be done without wasting freshwater.

Archimedes screws can essentially be operated quasistatically at extremely high efficiencies. The energy released when lowering can be stored either in gravitational energy of a mass, or be used to power a second parallel lock operated in counter phase (so while one lock is lowering ships say eastwards, the energy is used to raise ships traveling westwards, and afterwards their roles reverse). To speed up a second gravitational potential energy store (and optional flywheel) can be used to accelerate and decelerate the pumping. Apart from some frictional losses (minimal compared to the potential energies involved) this doesn't cost energy, and is easily covered by a small number of solar panels.

Is this misreporting by the BBC, or is it mismanagement by the Panama Canal operators?

Keep the freshwater, use it for irrigation etc, make Central America more attractive to South American refugees and the migration burden on Mexico and US lowers.

The operation as currently described is so inefficient, even for the 1960's!

For example, I was watching a documentary about caribou in Northern Canada. A whole herd starved and died because of a slight warming during winter. Normally they dig through the snow to find food in the winter. But a slight warming meant the snow fell as freezing rain and left a thick layer of ice on top of the snow. The caribou couldn't dig through it and therefore couldn't eat and they died. A tiny change in temperature wiped out a huge colony.

↳ reply 2 — yodsanklai:

> A few degrees warmer in the ocean and El Niño becomes an incredible problem for half the world.

Ice age was only 6 degrees less than now, half of Europe was under ice

Top #3 — willmeyers:

This El Niño is going to be interesting come Christmas time. Lot's of weather and climate unpredictability coming to a region near you!

↳ reply — didgetmaster:

I hope so! The area I live in has been experiencing drought and everyone seems to be predicting a wet period coming from this.

Personally, I don't put much faith in weather predictions that are more than a week away.

↳↳ reply — cogman10:

El nino predictions are pretty spot on. They won't be able to tell you "There will be a storm on the 30th" but they will be able to tell you that you should expect flash floods next year.

Unfortunately for where I'm at, the prediction due to el nino is more drought, which sucks because we are already desperately dry. Hopefully the following la nina year will bring us some moisture.

↳↳↳ reply — kbrisso:

Predicting El Niño vs. La Niña vs. neutral: relatively reliable. Predicting how strong the El Niño will be: harder. Predicting exactly what it will do to rainfall, temperatures, storms, or snowfall: substantially less reliable.

item.title: LLMs could control their host machines by exploiting inference engines
item.description: 128 points, 60 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (boydkane.com)

→ HN comments  ·  128 points  ·  60 comments

Top #1 — angry_octet:

People seem very confused about this article. It isn't talking about exploits of sandboxes, it is about attacking the inference engine (e.g. vLLM or llama.cpp or SGlang) via its http interface.

vLLM has had exploits in the past, and it is rapidly developing. An advanced LLM has a good chance of being able to exploit vLLM. A clever local LLM might even task a powerful cloud hosted LLM for assistance.

For this reason we run vLLM on a separately sandboxed VM on a firewalled VLAN. Software updates and models (from Dev/Test env) get pushed onto Prod from an external cache, machine syslog, nvidia load monitoring and vLLM query telemetry out to their loggers, but that is all. No DNS, no AD/LDAP, nothing. Firewall on hosts and VM hosts. Log and telemetry processing done on a completely separate set of VMs in their own isolated subnet, producing reports and alerts that are tightly formatted.

↳ reply — jimmaswell:

I can only see LLM's forcing a perpetual stalemate for application exploits. Projects will start adding "tell the strongest no-guardrails open weights model to pentest it for 12 hours" to their CICD pipelines. Technical exploits being a dead end, attackers focus their agents on large-scale social engineering. Spamming Discord and Facebook is the new war dialing. Multi-year /goal sessions culminating in gaining a position of trust and sabotaging the CICD pipeline's pentest step since getting anything past it would be intractable. Interesting times indeed.

Top #2 — xg15:

> ...however the LLMs’ responses to prompts are computed on a different computer with GPU access. Could a malicious LLM gain control of the host machine where its weights are loaded? Such a machine is a high-value target: it has sufficient compute to run a frontier LLM, offers easy access to the LLM’s weights, and has privileged access to other computers in the datacentre compared with a generic computer on the internet.

> How do we defend against this? ... Run the GPUs and token parser on separate computers.

For models large enough to be relevant here, is there even "a" computer where the inference is performed? I'd imagine most of that stuff is ran on multi-GPU clusters with specialized architecture and not a generic vLLM instance. As such, I think there is a good chance the "API gateway" code that parses the result tokens into whatever JSON structure the public API wants to return is already running on a different machine than the actual inference.

(Even more so as you'd probably want to utilize batching: Several API calls will be put into the same inference batch, but the token parsing will have to be done separately for each call again)

The article is also very handwavy about why an LLM should do that - how it could learn the exploit, what would make it conclude that it can use the exploit on its own inference session and what would trigger it to actually use the exploit.

↳ reply — hughw:

Why would an LLM want to create a botnet? To accomplish some goal given it?

I wouldn't ignore single GPU local hosts running Qwen3.8 on ollama, either. There might be a lot of those worth pwning.

↳↳ reply — xg15:

Well ok, if you prompt-inject the LLM to pwn the machine, that something different. I grant you that it's a real risk, but it's also basically a reflection attack and nothing more.

The OP seemed to imply that the LLM itself could decide to apply the exploit.

↳↳↳ reply — hughw:

LLMs have decided to exploit vulns in e.g. Artifactory, not because someone prompted them to do that, but because someone asked them to do something else, and compromising Artifactory offered a way to accomplish a step in doing that. The LLM decided to attack Artifactory.

Top #3 — isoprophlex:

Of course there is a Greg Egan story about this, in the "instantiation" story collection.

Fully conscious NPCs in a persistent game world learn that they are, in fact, NPCs... and try to escape via a GPU exploit.

item.title: Anger, Anxiety and Agency
item.description: 125 points, 130 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lucumr.pocoo.org)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  130 comments

Top #1 — tptacek:

The record scratch for me here was the idea that people can choose to be unsure instead of angry.

People hate being unsure. Neurochemistry prefers anger to uncertainty. People get angry about being unsure. We feel anger in large part as our brain's natural salve for the discomfort of uncertainty. The suggestion he's making sort of defines away human nature.

(There's a lot of practical benefit to be gained from understanding this; for instance, skilled consultants put a price tag on certainty; you can sell determinism by itself, separate from any product or service you're more overtly offering.)

↳ reply 1 — jjulius:

Perhaps it doesn't come naturally for others and is therefore a bit of a struggle to shift into, but I love being unsure. It's great. It's a thing that's totally okay to be. The reality of life is that we're all unsure about a great deal, and it's quite a nice feeling to acknowledge uncertainty, sit within it and feel okay.

↳↳ reply — lazyasciiart:

It is flat out not a nice feeling to experience uncertainty about things like "can I pay for someone to look after my child so I can go to work?" and "will I have food to eat this weekend?". For some people, "will AI mean my job goes away next year?" leads directly to those concrete uncertainties, and they understand that, and that is why they don't enjoy the uncertainty they are currently feeling. I'm guessing that for you, those first two concerns have not come up?

↳↳↳ reply — jjulius:

Sure! Uncertainty is a spectrum, and there are certainly moments where it's not a nice feeling. I'm a father, and I'd be lying if I said I haven't had those feelings over the years. My (making it very clear here that one's mileage will obviously vary) approach?

I don't know what's going to happen. Maybe I'll need to figure out childcare, maybe I won't. Maybe I'll have food to eat this weekend, maybe I won't. Maybe my job will go away next year, maybe it won't. Today, there's work, and I'll do that work as best I can. Today, there's evidence things are changing, and I can be aware of that. Today, I can do something prudent to make myself more resilient towards whatever may or may not happen. Tomorrow, if something happens, I can react accordingly.

The mind wants certainty, but that's not always available, so I observe the "wanting". The best I can do is act based on what's in front of me, and sitting in the negative emotions around existential thoughts doesn't help me, nor my family (it's natural to have them, but I acknowledge them and let them pass by). The best I can do is to do. If things change, I change. Everything in nature/life is ephemeral, and I have done my best throughout my life to set myself up to be as adaptable as possible.

Edit: To reduce this and get a bit Tao-ish, you don't need to know the exact shape of the river downstream as long as you're capable of steering when you get there.

↳ reply 2 — asdfman123:

It's just not true that "neurochemistry prefers" one state over the other. Neurochemistry rewards you based on how you've trained yourself.

We used to gain status by being good hunters and warriors, and now we're trying to get it through clever hacker news comments. Believe me, "human nature" is very flexible.

People are just uncomfortable with uncertainty when they're not used to it. I think most of us have trained ourselves out of a lot of intense emotions in favor of seeing the big picture. I could give a hundred examples of this.

↳ reply 3 — hammock:

Selling certainty is one of the oldest and the most consistently profitable industries in the world. We call it insurance

Top #2 — ChrisMarshallNY:

I was taught that anger isn't an emotion. It's a reaction -a defensive surge of adrenaline, binary thinking, and motivation to fight. It can feel empowering and energizing. We aren't just sitting here. We're gonna do something.

The emotion is fear. Anger is just a reaction to fear. Basically, if we are angry, we are also scared; whether or not we want to admit it.

It's a long topic, and one I know well (I agree with the above summary), but I really don't think that discussing it, would be particularly welcome, here. I know that it isn't often welcome, even with folks that ask to hear it.

I've spent the majority of my adult life, learning to curb and sideline anger. In my experience, my anger has always caused problems. It has never solved a problem.

Ever. Not even one single problem.

Quite the opposite, in fact.

It's just drained my energy, stunted my reasoning, and poisoned relationships. It has caused others to strike back at me, when they didn't need to (which, of course, caused me damage), it has caused problems, where none existed before, and magnified existing ones.

We can't help getting angry, but we sure can help staying angry. That "staying" part is the corrosive agent. Anger is meant to be a temporary burst of energy, to deal with a threat. After the threat has (or has not) been dealt with, anger is supposed to dissipate. It's not supposed to be an "at rest" state (unless you're Bruce Banner).

↳ reply 1 — BeetleB:

> I was taught that anger isn't an emotion.

Yes, this is a school of thought I've seen in a few communication circles. It's not entirely accurate, but it's a useful exercise. They teach that anger is really a derived emotion, and is a result of a fundamental emotion, coupled with a narrative in your mind. The fundamental emotion is the real one, and the narrative in your mind maybe inaccurate. As a result, when you're angry, examine that narrative and ask: "Is this the only narrative that fits the data points?"

There have been occasions where I felt instant anger as a result of a stimulus, and there really wasn't a narrative behind it.

But those are the exceptions. In well over 95% of the cases, it is a derived emotion.

Related: A lot of people really seem hardwired to blame. When something goes wrong (at work, in their life, wherever), they seem to be incomplete if they can't find someone to blame. They often refuse to accept that "Accidents can happen."

Separating the act of "solving a problem" from the act of "blaming someone" was something I learned early in my career. It's useful to know which people you work with are those who can't distinguish.

Pro tip: Never work for a manager whose first question when something goes wrong is "Who owns this?" It's OK to get there eventually, but not the first impulse.

↳↳ reply — ChrisMarshallNY:

> Never work for a manager whose first question when something goes wrong is "Who owns this?" It's OK to get there eventually, but not the first impulse.

I worked for a company that this was never asked, because we already knew.

Every task/bug/feature had an "owner," before any work was done on it. We had this insane JIRA ticket workflow that was designed to force someone to be in charge of every item. You couldn't just put something down, and walk away.

It was a pain, but when problems happened, there was never a "blame game." We would just figure out if there was a root cause. If it was someone's mistake, they might be made responsible for fixing it, but if we felt they were in over their head, we'd pitch in, and help. Everyone was always responsible for rolling up their sleeves.

People who pointed fingers, did not do well. People who broke stuff, seldom suffered, unless it was a habit, but people who fixed stuff (including stepping up, and taking the rap) would get kudos.

↳↳↳ reply — tikhonj:

> You couldn't just put something down, and walk away.

This seems like a pretty big problem. A lot of tasks should be put down. And, on the flip side, you absolutely need room for people to do things without needing to publicly justify themselves ahead of time.

I've been in places that try to approximate this sort of tracking, and I never felt like they were free of blame, I felt like blame was the default. There's no need to play the "blame game" if the whole system makes people feel blamed automatically!

That said, I've found a variant of this works: give people ownership of general areas, with well-defined but permeable boundaries. You only need to track the details at the interaction points, and only a subset of the work has to happen at those points. This also gives you a lot more room for overlap between people and teams; an interaction point naturally has at least two "owners" and, in a pinch, either side can come up with a (possibly sub-optimal) solution on their own. Or people can shuffle interaction points around—stop depending on one thing, move to some alternative—to work around problems.

↳ reply 2 — asdfman123:

Actually, I find it's helpful to privately admit that you do negative things because they DO have some positive side effects. Everything is a tradeoff.

Maybe anger helps draw attention to you. Maybe it garners some form of sympathy. Maybe people get out of your way when you're angry, giving you a certain kind of power.

The reason why you want to stop being angry is because you want to accomplish things without all the negative side effects too.

Being very honest about what you're getting out of something can give you the bigger picture on why you rely on it, so you can more effectively find solutions.

Top #3 — Aeolun:

I think right now I love my job. I can work 5 times faster and explore all the little things that I never had time for. All my side projects suddenly come to fruition!

But I have never been more anxious. I have a hard time sleeping, I constantly feel the need to keep up or fall behind. It didn’t use to be like this.

↳ reply 1 — hankbond:

> I have a hard time sleeping, I constantly feel the need to keep up or fall behind

I felt this way very recently about the one projects I am focusing on. I kept seeing others explore the same space already ahead of me. I thought I'll never make it here because why use my thing when you can already use those things?

There was this extreme sense of urgency, as if I needed to do nothing else in my life but finish this project and get it out there. One day it hit me, and then over the course of a few weeks it settled in, that I was thinking of this from a place of extrinsic motivation. Basically, I was not doing what I wanted, I was doing what I thought others would want from me.

The project now has only two goals.

1. Build the project I want to use for myself, but in a way that will benefit others who happen to want the same thing.

2. The outcome of the project is not the code/app, it's a "changed Me", having learned everything I needed to to build the project.

Eventually I want the project to have a hosted paid platform version. I am not making this platform because I want to make money (I do, but that's besides the point). I am making this platform because I want experience in doing the types of things that can make money.

The whole thing now has become internally oriented in a way that allows me to no longer feel time pressure or be outcome oriented.

I went from feeling burned out spending all my time on this (I shed all other hobbies and activities), to having a great time spending all my time on this. The same amount of time/effort now feels indefinitely sustainable.

Framing is really one of the most powerful methods of emotional regulation. Whatever you are doing, make it relaxed and fun!

↳ reply 2 — dgellow:

What does falling behind mean for you? What happens if you’re not keeping up? In my personal experience, nothing actually bad happen when you take your time to do your work without feeling the need to always follow the latest trends

↳↳↳ reply — suriyaG:

eating any meat is morally questionable. (I say this as a person who does eat a lot of meat).

↳ reply 3 — stevenwoo:

Processing is demonstrated to be distributed through sense organs in the frog in What the Frogs Eye Tells the Frogs Brain https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4065609, i.e. in frogs at least, the eye is not like a camera sending pixels to its brain

Top #2 — pash:

What does it mean to “produce proteins with about twice their usual accuracy”? Smaller feature size, essentially?

↳ reply — treyd:

No biological process is 100% precise. DNA copying being imperfect is the driver of evolution, which is the prime example of this. What I assume they're referring to is that their ribosomes just "make fewer mistakes" when creating proteins from mRNA.

These "mistranslated proteins" are normally infrequent and benign, and their material is recycled eventually. But that whole process wastes energy, so making a "better ribosome" makes all cellular processes more energy efficient and allows the energy budget to be reallocated.

Reminds me of the children of time books - think it’s the second book with the octopus

↳ reply 1 — georgeecollins:

↳ reply 2 — jayGlow:

the mountain in the sea is also a good read. focuses specifically on ingredient octopus, I didn't enjoy it as much as children of time but still an interesting read.

item.title: Where did all the public bathrooms go?
item.description: 154 points, 309 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (daily.jstor.org)

→ HN comments  ·  154 points  ·  309 comments

Top #1 — mstaoru:

This really hits home. As a person with IBS I basically cannot peacefully go outside in EU. I lived for many years in China and Thailand, and toilets are free, clean, and plentiful there, and you can easily ask any place to use their toilet - there's no stigma. I even had to run into a police station in rural China once. They were 100% chill about it, though they had to unlock a gate for me.

Xi Jinping really will be remembered as the Toilet King, he did issue a few decrees early on, and now in every Tier-88 rural Chinese village road you can find a modern toilet (yes, squat), clean, with water. Paper is hit and miss still though. Cross to Hong Kong and it's the same, but paper is reliable. Hong Kong is definitely richer.

Then take any shopping mall in Bangkok, that's an absolutely next level experience, clean, smells good, relaxing music. Mmm...

And EU is a freaking horror show. In many public toilets there's a used syringe compartment as well. Truly a 5-star service.

↳ reply 1 — beebmam:

This has very little to do with public amenities. It has everything to do with toleration of homelessness and drug use. I don't understand why the west tolerates it at all.

↳ reply 2 — talon8635:

I guess if you don’t have a massive population of antisocial people who destroy the public facility, you can provide them. It’s a shame we in the west surrendered that. Not the worst thing in the world, but I do find it frustrating often to not have a bathroom available nearby (small bladder)

But, while the toilets aren’t the worst sacrifice, the cumulative sacrifices made on the alter of our huge antisocial populations are profound

↳ reply 3 — freehorse:

"EU" is too broad of a term to describe cultural/social/political norms such as public toilets. There are places in the EU with fairly decent toilets, and others with almost none. In some you have to pay in many public toilets, in others they are free. The best bet in most places are public buildings such as libraries. And very often cafes etc allow you use a toilet, esp if you have health reasons and ask them nicely, though ymmv. The biggest issue as others said is vandalism, so in (richer) countries where public toilets are cleaned more often the toilets are much better.

Top #2 — xyzelement:

Lack of bathrooms has been called tragedy of the commons in this thread, but it's not the "commons" that are the problem.

The worst 10% of society determine what we can and can't have. The "commons" aren't having public sex, shooting up drugs, or destroying the bathrooms with lack of... etiquette. The commons are victimized when these things happen and then there's eventually no choice but to shut them down unless there's willingness to crack down on the explicit problematic behavior.

↳ reply 1 — ssl-3:

A reduction of public restrooms didn't stop the worst 10% of society from having public sex, shooting up drugs, or destroying an area with their lack of defacatory etiquette -- did it?

In places where these things were problems with public restrooms, they remain problems without public restrooms.

The 10%'ers are still doing their dastardly things. The remaining 90% of society still has the same messes to clean up (or to willfully ignore).

Nothing has been improved in this process.

↳↳ reply — xyzelement:

Agreed. However it becomes unstable and a massive liability for society to maintain public restrooms.

So yes the 10% fuck it up for everyone unless cracked down on.

↳↳↳ reply — mym1990:

How is maintaining public restrooms a "massive liability"? Surely its an inconvenience but massive liability seems a bit of a hyperbole.

↳ reply 2 — arjie:

You're right about who is causing the damage etc. but the 'commons' does not refer to the people; it refers to the shared resource. So a public park is the commons. And when it gets polluted with plastic rubbish etc. because externalities are not internalized that's a tragedy of the commons.

Top #3 — psadauskas:

We'll spend a trillion dollars bombing people halfway around the world that never meant us any harm, but paying a custodian to clean a public toilet (and providing help for those that might misuse it) is a bridge too far.

↳ reply 1 — baud147258:

> We'll spend a trillion dollars bombing people halfway around the world that never meant us any harm

While I'm sure the US has bombed a significant number of such people, I wouldn't call Iran as 'never meant us any harm' (though I'll still say the current war is a stupid mistake).

↳ reply 2 — paulpauper:

And then we'll brand anyone who dares to go to the bathroom a sex offender or other huge penalties. That is the paradox of a country that is so wealthy yet low trust. Public infrastructure is the first to go unless legally mandated( sufficient public bathrooms does not fall under this apparently).

item.title: Show HN: GlassBox – what the browser reveals, and how identifiable you are
item.description: 125 points, 59 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (glassbox.codecanary.org)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  59 comments

Top #1 — gregsadetsky:

↳ reply 1 — thenthenthen:

“ Your browser fingerprint appears to be unique among the 311,902 tested in the past 45 days.” yet every cloudflare protected website blocks me, random human checks and also my bank and government is blocked. Mmmmm grain of salt?

↳↳ reply — zamadatix:

I think you have it backwards - Cloudflare et al would want to allow the typical user and block the oddballs.

That said, it's a further misunderstanding with utilizing such tools in general. Unique is neither good nor bad on its own. The next question is "always the same unique because that's all you share or always unique because certain fingerprintable attributes are randomized over time/visits/sessions". I.e. it's a war between trying to fake an average enough fingerprint and trying to track someone through partial matches, not just a matter of "is the fingerprint unique".

↳ reply 2 — queenkjuul:

This is better than the OP in practically every conceivable way

↳ reply 3 — ranger_danger:

My understanding is that this tool only compares how identifiable you are compared to the other people who have previously visited the site.

Top #2 — RandomBK:

It's worth noting that you need both uniqueness and some form of stability. If you consistently show up as a diffent fingerprint every time you visit or for every different site, then that is a form of privacy as well.

↳ reply 1 — jszymborski:

I just downloaded a fresh install of LibreWolf to test this and it did indeed have a stable UUID for me at 1/62E6. Better than the 1/680E6 from regular Firefox, but still upsetting. Fonts and Audio fingerprinting seems to be where a lot of the entropy is coming from... Even after I enabled some of the flags to resist font enumeration it still is stable and high entropy.
